title: The clay lamp
hookLine: a thief took his iron lamp, so he bought a clay one, and the thief lost more (Discourses 1.18)

cards: Someone takes the package off your porch. Or your bike, or your lunch from the office fridge. It's small, but it stings for days.
You replay it, check the doorbell camera, tell five people.
Epictetus had something stolen too, and his reaction is one of the most well-known little stories in the Discourses: a noise at the window, an empty spot by the shrine, and a cheaper replacement.

teach.b: It's still Discourses book one, chapter eighteen, right after the teaching about blindness. I kept an iron lamp, Epictetus tells his students, beside the little shrine of my household gods.
I heard a noise at the window, ran down, and found it gone. Then I thought it over. The thief wanted a lamp; that's understandable.
So tomorrow, I told myself, you'll find a clay one. A person only loses what they have. Notice the arithmetic.
An iron lamp was a decent possession; a clay lamp costs very little and gives the same light. Epictetus lost almost nothing that mattered.

teach.h: FOR A LAMP, HE BECAME A THIEF.
teach.b: The thief, as Epictetus sees it elsewhere in the Discourses, paid far more: for a lamp, he became a thief. He gave up his own honesty, which no one could have taken from him, for a piece of iron. Who lost more?
Epictetus also explains why thieves make us so angry: we admire the things they take. If you didn't prize your clothes so much, he says, you wouldn't rage at the one who steals them.
And there's a funny ending from outside the Discourses.

teach.h: THE CLAY LAMP SOLD FOR A FORTUNE.
teach.b: The writer Lucian, a generation later, mocks a man who paid three thousand drachmas for Epictetus' clay lamp after the philosopher died, as if owning it would make him wise.
The cheap lamp became an expensive treasure, exactly the kind of admiring Epictetus warned about.

how: Many readers keep Epictetus' clay lamp as a shorthand for letting small losses go: replacing what's gone simply and refusing to give up their own calm or character over it.

games.q: you're Epictetus. you run downstairs at a noise and find your iron lamp stolen. what do you do?
o: report it and bar the windows.
tell yourself: tomorrow you'll find a clay one.
games.why: he decided to buy a cheap clay lamp, reasoning that a person only loses what they have.

practice: Think of one small thing taken from you, recently or long ago: an object, some money, credit for your work, a seat, and notice how tightly you still hold it.
Ask what your clay lamp would be here, the simple, cheap thing that gives the same light. Then rest on what you still have that no one could take.

wordCard.voice: Lychnos. Greek for the lamp Epictetus lost: an iron one, replaced for a little with a cheap clay lychnos, while the thief gave up his own honesty.

orig.note: Greek lychnos: an oil lamp, the kind Epictetus kept by his household shrine.

carryVoice: Your line: a clay lamp. The light was never in the iron. That's day four hundred two.
